Multifamily Marketing Metrics That Predict Leases (and the Ones That Don't)

Nov 2, 2026Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM6 min read
Key takeaways
  • Cost per lease by source, read with tour to lease conversion, tells you more than any other single number.
  • Cost per lead is only useful next to lease data. A cheap lead that never tours costs more than it looks.
  • Unbranded search visibility, Google Maps visibility and tours booked are the leading indicators to watch.
  • Report weekly, date every number, and compare each week with the previous four before acting.
In this article
  1. What is the lead to tour to lease funnel?
  2. Why is cost per lease better than cost per lead?
  3. What is a good tour conversion rate?
  4. Why does attribution miss so many leases?

The multifamily marketing metrics that predict leases are the ones closest to a renter's decision: tours, tour to lease conversion, cost per lease, and how often you appear when renters search without your name. Impressions, followers and rankings for your own brand describe activity, not demand, and rarely show whether next month's leases are coming.

Most reports I review lead with the second group because those numbers are large and usually go up. Owners deserve a report that starts with the first group.

What is the lead to tour to lease funnel?

The funnel is the path from first contact to signed lease: a lead is any renter who reaches out, a tour is a scheduled or completed visit, and a lease is a signed application that moves in. Each step has a conversion rate, and the gaps between steps show where you are losing renters.

Put plainly, the three numbers to track for each community are:

  • Lead to tour rate. The share of leads that book a tour. A low rate often means slow follow up or missing information.
  • Tour to lease rate. The share of tours that end in a signed lease. A low rate often points to price, product or the tour.
  • Lead to lease rate. The full funnel in one number, useful for comparing sources.

Track them by source and by week, because a blended monthly rate hides the weak source.

Why is cost per lease better than cost per lead?

Cost per lease divides what you spent on a source by the leases it produced, so it measures what you actually bought. Cost per lead only measures how cheaply a source produces contacts, and cheap contacts that never tour can be the most expensive line in the budget.

Here is simple arithmetic, not client data. Source A costs $20 a lead and sends 100 leads, 2 of which lease, so it costs $1,000 per lease. Source B costs $60 a lead and sends 30 leads, 6 of which lease, so it costs $300 per lease. On a cost per lead report, Source A looks three times better. On a cost per lease report, it is more than three times worse.

MetricWhat it tells youPredicts leases?
Cost per leaseWhat a signed lease costs by sourceYes, it is the outcome
Tour to lease rateHow well tours closeYes
Tours bookedDemand that is close to a decisionYes, within weeks
Unbranded search and Maps visibilityWhether new renters can find youYes, as a leading signal

What is a good tour conversion rate?

There is no single good tour conversion rate, because it depends on your market, price position, concessions and whether you are in lease up or stabilized. The useful comparison is your own rate over time and across sources, read alongside what competitors are offering that week.

I am wary of anyone who quotes a universal benchmark here. A drop after a rent increase means something different from the same drop after your best leasing agent leaves. Ask what changed on site before blaming marketing, and the reverse.

Why does attribution miss so many leases?

Attribution misses leases because renters touch several channels before they contact you, and the last one recorded gets the credit. Listing sites, phone calls and walk ins are the three biggest blind spots,

  • ILS leads. In an Apartments.com survey reported by the National Apartment Association, 85% of renters said they use or plan to use a listing site like Apartments.com. Many of them searched Google or read your reviews first, and the listing site still gets the credit. We cover this in why apartment communities need more than ILS leads.
  • Calls. The Calls number in your Google Business Profile counts taps on the call button. Google's Business Profile performance reference describes it as the number of times the call button was clicked. A tap is not a conversation, and a renter who dials your number by hand is not counted at all.
  • Walk ins. A renter who drove past, looked you up on Maps and walked in often gets logged as "drive by" or nothing. Ask your leasing team how they record the source, and whether they ask.

You will not close these gaps completely. Know where they are, so a source is not cut because its leases were credited elsewhere.

Which metrics predict leases before they happen?

Unbranded search visibility and Google Maps visibility are the best leading indicators I know, because they measure whether renters who have never heard of you can find you. Leases trail them by weeks, so a slide in either one is an early warning while there is still time to act.

Renters usually start without a name. In the same Apartments.com survey reported by NAA, 87% of more than 15,000 adults planning to rent had no specific property in mind when they started looking. The searches that matter are "two bedroom apartments near" a place, not your name.

Maps matters because so many of those searches are local. Check your position across the trade area where renters search, not from the leasing office, against your true competitors. Our post on why apartments lose tours in Google Maps goes deeper on reading this.

Which multifamily metrics are vanity metrics?

Impressions, follower counts and rankings for your own community name are vanity metrics when they are reported alone. They can rise while tours fall, and none of them shows whether a renter who did not already know you found you and acted.

  • Impressions count how often something was shown, not whether anyone noticed it.
  • Followers are mostly current residents, staff and vendors. That audience helps retention, but it is not a leasing pipeline.
  • Branded rankings are almost always strong. Ranking first for your own name tells you the renter already knew you.

None of these is useless. They become useful next to a number closer to a lease.

What should a weekly marketing report include?

A useful weekly report fits on one page per community, dates every number, and connects visibility to tours and leases. It should say what changed, what we think caused it, and the single next action, including when something did not work.

  1. Leads, tours and leases for the week, by source, with the dates covered.
  2. Tour to lease rate and cost per lease by source, trailing four weeks.
  3. Unbranded search visibility and its trend.
  4. Maps position across the trade area against named competitors.
  5. Google profile actions such as calls, website clicks and direction requests, labeled for what they actually count.
  6. What changed this week, what competitors changed, and one next step.

One week is not a trend, so read each week against the last four before acting.

Questions we hear

What is the most important multifamily marketing metric?

Cost per lease by source, read with tour to lease conversion. Together they show what a signed lease actually costs and whether the problem sits in marketing or on site.

Is cost per lead a useful metric for apartments?

Only next to lease data. A source with cheap leads can cost far more per lease if those leads rarely tour or sign, so judge sources on cost per lease.

What are leading indicators for apartment leasing?

Unbranded search visibility, Google Maps visibility across your trade area, and tours booked. They move before leases do, which gives you time to adjust pricing, offers or spend.

Why do Google Business Profile calls not match our call logs?

Google counts taps on the call button, not completed conversations, and it misses renters who dial by hand. Compare the profile count with answered calls from your phone records.

How often should multifamily marketing be reported?

Weekly, with each number dated and compared against the prior four weeks. Monthly reporting tends to arrive after a problem has already cost you leases.
